concepts.title: Development as Political Contestation
concepts.definition: Decisions about development are not technical puzzles that experts alone can settle: building a steel plant on tribal iron-ore land weighs one social group's livelihood against another's, the present against the future, and jobs against environment -- so in a democracy the final call belongs to elected representatives, not to markets or experts.
concepts.key_idea: Whose need counts as the nation's need is itself a political question; every development choice creates winners, losers and a legitimate debate.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps203.txt POSCO case and Political contestation (lines 41-149)
question_patterns: why are development decisions described as political and not merely technical
identify the conflicting interests in the orissa steel plant dispute
who should take the final decision on a project that displaces people and why
how can development mean different things to different sections of people
what makes the choice between jobs and environment a democratic question
explain the role of people's representatives in deciding major projects

solution_steps.explain: the state hoping for investment, the company seeking ore, tribal residents fearing displacement, environmentalists fearing pollution and the Centre guarding investor confidence

solution_steps.action: show why expertise cannot settle it
solution_steps.explain: weighing one group against another or one generation against the next is a value judgement, not a calculation an expert can deliver
advice from miners, environmentalists and economists informs, but people's representatives in touch with public feeling must take or approve the final decision

concepts.title: Ideas of Development: Modernisation and Two Rival Models
concepts.definition: Post-Independence debate treated development as becoming modern, usually measured against the industrialised West, but India stood before two ready-made routes: the liberal-capitalist model of Europe and the US and the socialist model of the USSR; with communists, socialists and Nehru alike impressed by Soviet growth, the socialist model had the stronger following and left meant state control while right meant free markets.
concepts.key_idea: Development is an idea with politics inside it -- which model you pick decides who owns industry and who answers for redistribution.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps203.txt Ideas of development, Left and Right box (lines 150-210)
question_patterns: what did becoming modern mean in the development debate of the 1950s
compare the liberal capitalist and socialist models open to india
why did the soviet model attract indian leaders across parties
distinguish between left and right ideologies regarding the economy
why does any discussion of development generate conflict and debate
how did the national movement shape india's view of the state's economic role

solution_steps.explain: development meant growth, material progress and scientific rationality on the western pattern, letting nations be labelled developed, developing or underdeveloped
liberal-capitalism relied on private ownership and markets; the socialist model relied on state ownership and planning, exemplified by the USSR
the national movement had already fixed poverty alleviation and redistribution as government responsibility, and leaders from the Communist Party, Socialist Party and Nehru favoured the Soviet path

concepts.title: Planning, the Planning Commission and the Bombay Plan
concepts.definition: Because development could not be left to private actors, India set up a Planning Commission in March 1950 by a simple government resolution -- not by the Constitution -- with the Prime Minister as chairperson and an advisory role whose plans needed Cabinet approval; the impulse crossed political lines, as shown by the Bombay Plan of 1944 in which big industrialists themselves asked the state to lead industrial investment.
concepts.key_idea: From left to right, planning was the obvious choice: even industrialists wanted the state to take the major economic initiatives.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps203.txt Planning, Planning Commission and Bombay Plan boxes (lines 211-305)
question_patterns: why was a planning commission preferred over leaving development to markets
how was the planning commission set up and what powers did it have
what was the bombay plan and who drafted it
why is the planning commission not a constitutional body
what experiences around the world encouraged planning in the 1940s and 1950s
explain the advisory character of the planning commission under the prime minister

solution_steps.explain: depression-era lessons, postwar reconstruction and Soviet growth made state-led planning respectable worldwide, and Indian industrialists signed the 1944 Bombay Plan seeking state initiative
created in March 1950 by government resolution, chaired by the Prime Minister, advisory in nature, effective only when the Union Cabinet approved its recommendations
its charter tied planning to the Directive Principles -- livelihood for all, common-good distribution of resources and prevention of concentration of wealth

concepts.title: Five Year Plans and the Plan-Non-Plan Budget Divide
concepts.definition: Indian planning copied the Soviet device of five year plans: a document fixing government income and expenditure for five years, with budgets split into a non-plan part for routine yearly spending and a plan part spent on five-year priorities; excitement peaked with the Second Plan of 1956 and faded by the Fourth, when crisis forced a plan holiday in 1966.
concepts.key_idea: The five-year horizon let government act on the larger picture, but plan enthusiasm could not survive the economic crisis of the mid-1960s.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps203.txt The Early Initiatives, First FYP document (lines 306-363)
question_patterns: what is a five year plan and why did india adopt it
distinguish between plan and non plan expenditure in the budget
what advantage does a five year plan give a government
why did india declare a plan holiday in 1966
how did public excitement around planning rise and fall
what criticisms were levelled at the early five year plans

solution_steps.explain: the plan document covers all central and state income and expenditure for five years so governments can make long-term interventions
non-plan spending meets routine annual items while plan spending follows the priorities fixed by the plan
the First Plan of December 1951 was widely debated, excitement crested with the Second Plan in 1956 and persisted into the Third, but the 1966 crisis led to a plan holiday

concepts.title: First Plan versus Second Plan: Agriculture First or Industry First
concepts.definition: The First Plan (1951-1956) preached patience -- K. N. Raj's hasten slowly -- concentrating on dams, irrigation and land reform to revive agriculture hit by Partition; the Second Plan (1956), drafted under P. C. Mahalanobis after the Avadi resolution on a socialist pattern of society, chased rapid industrialisation through heavy industry, import tariffs and a dominant public sector, but bred foreign-exchange strain, food worries and an urban bias.
concepts.key_idea: The first plan guarded rural livelihoods while the second gambled on structural transformation, and the tension between feeding people and building factories never fully disappeared.
concepts.textbook_ref: leps203.txt The First Five Year Plan, Rapid Industrialisation (lines 339-523)
question_patterns: what was the major thrust of the first five year plan
how did the second plan differ from the first in strategy
what did the avadi session resolve and how did it shape the second plan
explain the role of p c mahalanobis in indian planning
why did land reforms matter so much to the first plan
what problems did rapid industrialisation create for the economy

solution_steps.explain: hasten slowly was the watchword: investment in dams and irrigation, land reform against unequal land distribution, and an effort to lift savings for higher national income
Mahalanobis's team pushed simultaneous structural change -- heavy industries like steel, railways and machinery in the public sector, protected behind import tariffs
technology imports drained foreign exchange, industry-first allocation raised food shortage fears, the Third Plan repeated the urban bias, and critics demanded agriculture-related industry instead

worked_examples.question_pattern: Villagers of three gram panchayats protest outside a Korean company's office against a steel plant signed with the state government. Identify the interests at stake and say who should finally decide.

solution_template.explain: the state wants capital and jobs, the company wants ore and land, villagers fear displacement from homes and livelihood, environmentalists fear pollution
there is no expert formula to weigh tribal livelihood against industrial investment; it is a conflict of values
people's representatives, advised by experts and approved by the public, must take the decision in a democracy

worked_examples.source_ref: leps203.txt The First Five Year Plan and Rapid Industrialisation
worked_examples.question_pattern: A plan document urges dams and land reform while its successor imposes tariffs and expands public-sector steel. Which plans are these and what distinguishes them?

solution_template.explain: dams, irrigation and land reform as the key to growth belong to the First Plan of 1951-1956 under the hasten slowly counsel of K. N. Raj
tariffs protecting industry plus public-sector heavy industry reflect the Second Plan of 1956 drafted under Mahalanobis after the Avadi resolution
patience in agriculture versus rapid structural transformation through industry is the core difference
